title: What’s Missing in AGN Feedback?Lessons learnt from Magneticum, IllustrisTNG and Simba

paper.title: What’s Missing in AGN Feedback? Lessons learnt from Magneticum, IllustrisTNG and Simba
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims. Accurately balancing gas reservoirs, star formation, and feedback processes across cosmic time remains one of the central challenges for galaxy formation models implemented in modern hydrodynamical simulations. While different feedback prescriptions can reproduce selected local galaxy properties with varying success, some of the most pronounced discrepancies emerge when comparing predictions for the hot gas content of dark matter halos. Methods. In this study, we examine three state-of-the-art cosmological simulations: Magneticum, IllustrisTNG, and SIMBA, which struggle to simultaneously reproduce the observed galaxy and halo gas properties in the local Universe. We confront their predictions with spatially resolved galaxy data from MaNGA and recent observational constraints on the hot gas mass fraction–halo mass ( f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{\mathrm{h}} ) relation derived from eROSITA and Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (SZ) measurements. Results. Reproducing the observed relation f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{\mathrm{h}} requires strong active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback. However, such strong feedback often leads to excessive quenching in simulated galaxy populations. Magneticum and SIMBA successfully match the observed gas fraction relation but predict an overabundance of quenched galaxies. In contrast, IllustrisTNG implements comparatively weaker AGN feedback, yielding more realistic star-forming fractions but systematically overpredicting hot gas masses in massive groups and poor clusters. Conclusions. In general, the stated tensions indicate that the current feedback models remain incomplete, not only in terms of the total energy injected but also in terms of the timing, location and coupling of this energy to the surrounding gas. Our results, therefore, highlight the need to revisit subgrid feedback prescriptions and to develop more self-consistent models capable of simultaneously regulating galaxy growth and the thermodynamic properties of halo gas. Motivated by this discrepancy, a companion study will explore whether the feedback strengths required to match halo gas constraints inevitably lead to overquenching and distorted galaxy demographics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Understanding how galaxies and their host halos co-evolve requires a consistent picture of the baryonic cycle across a wide mass range, from Milky Way–sized halos to massive clusters. It is well established that low-mass halos predominantly host star-forming galaxies, while massive halos tend to host quenched systems. This trend suggests that star formation is regulated by a transition from stellar feedback-dominated processes at low masses to AGN-driven quenching at high masses ( Dekel and Silk 1986 ; Kauffmann et al. 2004 ; Hopkins et al. 2012 , e.g.,) . In the galaxy group mass range (i.e. ≈ 10 13 − 14 ​ M ⊙ \approx 10^{13-14}M_{\odot} ), classical models predicted that galaxy groups retain a large fraction of their baryons in the hot intragroup medium (IGrM). In contrast, recent observational studies including X-ray measurements from eROSITA reveal that galaxy groups with halo masses 10 12 − 14 ​ M ⊙ 10^{12-14}M_{\odot} are strongly depleted in hot gas relative to the cosmic baryon fraction ( Zhang et al. 2025 ; Popesso, P. et al. 2026 ) . These systems retain only ≈ ( 20 CLOSE \approx(20 – OPEN 40 ) % 40)\% of the expected baryons within R 200 R_{200} 1 1 1 R 200 R_{200} the radius enclosing a mean density 200 times the critical density of the Universe. , implying that feedback processes redistribute baryons far beyond the virial region. Independent constraints from the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel’dovich (kSZ) effect also indicate that halo gas profiles are significantly more extended than predicted by standard models ( Hadzhiyska et al. 2025 ; Bigwood et al. 2026 ; Siegel et al. 2026 ) . In particular, Siegel et al. (2026) combine X-ray gas fractions with kSZ measurements over 13 < log 10 ⁡ ( M 500 / M ⊙ ) < 14 13<\log_{10}(M_{500}/M_{\odot})<14 and infer that strong feedback suppresses the matter power spectrum by ≈ 10 ± 2 % \approx 10\pm 2\% at k = 1 ​ h ​ Mpc − 1 k=1\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc^{-1}} , consistent with baryons being displaced to large radii. Additional support for extended baryon reservoirs comes from fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures, which probe the integrated electron column density along extragalactic sightlines ( Lanman et al. 2026 ) . Despite these observational indications of strong baryon redistribution, cosmological hydrodynamical simulations often struggle to reproduce the low gas fractions inferred for galaxy groups. Most models rely on subgrid prescriptions for black hole accretion and AGN feedback that operate below the resolution scale, introducing uncertainties in the predicted thermodynamic structure of halo gas ( Puchwein and Springel 2013 ; Weinberger et al. 2017 ; Schulze et al. 2018 ) . Moreover, simulations are typically calibrated to match the galaxy stellar mass function ( Vogelsberger et al. 2014 ; Schaye et al. 2015 ) , while hot-gas properties are often tuned using X-ray–selected samples biassed toward gas-rich systems ( McCarthy et al. 2010 ; McCarthy et al. 2017 ; Schaye and others 2023 ) . Such samples exclude the X-ray-faint populations identified in volume-limited eROSITA surveys ( Marini et al. 2024 ; Popesso et al. 2025 ) , leading many simulations to overpredict the hot gas content of group-scale halos despite reproducing galaxy statistics near the Milky-Way mass scale ( Shreeram et al. 2025 ) . Among current simulation suites, the Magneticum simulations provide an alternative approach. Their feedback parameters are chosen to reproduce cluster scaling relations and the Magorrian relation rather than explicitly tuning the stellar mass function ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) . Nevertheless, Magneticum has been shown to reproduce several key observed galaxy properties, including the stellar mass function over a broad stellar-mass range, the mass–metallicity relation, and the cosmic star-formation history ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) . Furthermore, Magneticum reproduces several hot-gas observables, including gas fractions and luminosity–mass relations, in close agreement with eROSITA measurements ( Dolag et al. 2016 ; Dolag et al. 2025 ; Toptun et al. 2025 ; Popesso, P. et al. 2026 ) . A key goal of this work is to assess whether this success also extends to reproducing the observed distribution of galaxy populations in the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane, their AGN activity, and their environmental dependence. This issue is closely tied to the co-evolution of AGN and their host galaxies. The hot gas constitutes the dominant baryonic reservoir in massive halos, and its cooling within the circum-galactic region can provide a sustained fuel supply for star formation. This process is particularly important in galaxy groups and clusters, where gas accretion occurs predominantly in the hot mode. In this regime, central galaxies are no longer fed by cold gas streams from cosmic web filaments, as these are unable to penetrate the hot halo ( Dekel and Birnboim 2006 ) . Consequently, the thermodynamical state of the hot gas and its regulation by AGN feedback play a key role in controlling the star formation activity of massive galaxies. In this work, we compare three state-of-the-art cosmological hydrodynamical simulations: IllustrisTNG ( Pillepich et al. 2018a ; Nelson et al. 2018 ) , SIMBA ( Davé et al. 2019 ) , and Magneticum ( Dolag et al. 2016 ; Dolag et al. 2025 ) . The comparison is motivated by their markedly different levels of agreement with current measurements of the f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{\mathrm{h}} relation from X-ray and kSZ observations: Magneticum shows the closest agreement, SIMBA provides an intermediate match, while IllustrisTNG exhibits the largest discrepancy ( Popesso, P. et al. 2026 ) . These simulations adopt different implementations of AGN feedback, ranging from dual-mode thermal and kinetic feedback in IllustrisTNG ( Weinberger et al. 2017 ; Pillepich et al. 2018a ) , jet-driven and X-ray feedback in SIMBA ( Davé et al. 2019 ) , and a highly efficient thermal feedback model in Magneticum ( Dolag et al. 2016 ; Dolag et al. 2025 ) . Taken together, they provide a controlled framework for testing whether models that successfully reproduce the hot gas content of halos can also recover the observed distribution of galaxy properties. To enable a fair and robust comparison between simulations and observations, we adopt the f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{\mathrm{h}} relations from Popesso, P. et al. (2026) and Siegel et al. (2026) (see appendix Fig. 9 ), and use MaNGA as our primary low-redshift benchmark for galaxy properties. MaNGA provides spatially resolved integral-field spectroscopy for a statistically representative sample of nearby galaxies with stellar masses M ⋆ > 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{10}\,M_{\odot} , enabling accurate measurements of star formation rates (SFR) and stellar masses while minimising aperture biases. Its dense sampling of group environments, where the majority of galaxies reside in the local Universe, makes it particularly well suited for comparisons with cosmological simulations. The structure of this paper is as follows. In Section 2 we describe the observational data and simulation samples. Section 3 examines the distribution of galaxies on the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane and compares quenching fractions between observations and simulations. Section 4 investigates the distribution of AGN activity, while Section 5 explores the environmental dependence of galaxy evolution. Finally, Section 6 summarises our results and conclusively highlighting their implications for models of baryon cycling in the local Universe. We assume flat Λ \Lambda CDM cosmological parameters: H 0 = 70 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , Ω m = 0.3 \Omega_{\rm m}=0.3 and Ω Λ = 0.7 \Omega_{\Lambda}=0.7 . To ensure consistency between simulations and observations, all are rescaled to a Chabrier (2003) initial mass function (IMF).

sections.heading: 2 Data sample
sections.text: This section describes both the observational and simulated data sets used in this study. Each dataset is well described in its respective section to classify galaxies in terms of star formation activity, nuclear activity, and environment.

sections.heading: 2.1 The observational dataset: MaNGA sample
sections.text: The Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA), part of SDSS-IV ( Law et al. 2015 ; Blanton et al. 2017 ) , is an optical integral field unit (IFU) survey providing spatially resolved spectroscopy for more than 10,000 galaxies in the redshift range 0.01 < z < 0.15 0.01<z<0.15 ( Bundy et al. 2015 ; Abdurro’uf et al. 2022 ) . Its wavelength coverage (3,600–10,300 Å) and spatial extent (typically ≥ 1.5 ​ R e \geq 1.5\,R_{e} ) enable spatially resolved measurements of stellar mass, star formation rate (SFR), and emission-line diagnostics across galaxy discs ( Wake et al. 2017 ; Comerford et al. 2020 ; Comerford et al. 2024 ) . We use the Pipe3D value-added catalogue for the MaNGA DR17 release ( Sánchez et al. 2022b ) . Integrated stellar masses ( M ⋆ M_{\star} ) are obtained by summing the stellar mass surface density ( Σ ⋆ \Sigma_{\star} ) derived from single stellar population (SSP) fits over unmasked spaxels. We also extract SFRs, spectroscopic redshifts ( z z ), and luminosity distances ( D L D_{L} ). SFR estimates are based on the mean of SSP fits over 10, 32, and 100 Myr timescales and are consistent with SFR H ​ α \mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{H\alpha}} measurements ( Sánchez et al. 2022b ) . AGN identifications are supplemented using the MaNGA-AGN related catalogues of Comerford et al. (2020) ; Comerford et al. (2024) . Starting from the initial 10,220 MaNGA sources, we apply a quality cut ( QCFLAG = 0 \mathrm{QCFLAG}=0 ) following Sánchez et al. (2022b) , leaving 9,828 reliable galaxies. To ensure stellar-mass completeness and robust spectroscopic measurements, we further restrict the sample to log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) > 10 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})>10 and z < 0.085 z<0.085 following Popesso et al. (2019b) and ensuring reliable SDSS redshifts ( Renzini and Peng 2015 ) . This threshold lies above the regime where MaNGA volume-completeness corrections diverge at log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≃ 9.75 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\simeq 9.75 ( Fraser-McKelvie and Cortese 2022 ) . A recent analysis based on the same Pipe3D dataset confirms the completeness of the sample in this stellar mass range ( de Isídio et al. 2026 ) . Moreover, this mass regime corresponds to the characteristic turnover mass associated with AGN feedback and galaxy quenching ( Popesso et al. 2019b ; Popesso et al. 2023 ) suitable for our AGN study. The final primary sample contains 6,709 galaxies ( ≈ 68.30 % \approx 68.30\% of the 9,828 quality-selected objects). Pipe3D adopts an initial mass function (IMF) by default of Salpeter ( Ellison et al. 2024 ) .

sections.heading: 2.1.1 AGN classification and Multi-wavelength catalogue
sections.text: AGN feedback studies require identification across the electromagnetic spectrum ( Comerford et al. 2020 ; Escott et al. 2026 ) , as emission spans the entire electromagnetic spectrum, giving a window of different physics ( Padovani et al. 2017 ) . We therefore adopt a multi-wavelength approach to capture diverse accretion modes. Our catalogue combines MaNGA-based AGN from the public pyPipe3D optical AGN candidate catalogue ( S AGN S_{\rm AGN} ; 227; Sánchez et al. 2022a ) 2 2 2 https://ifs.astroscu.unam.mx/MaNGA/Pipe3D_v3_1_1/tables/AGNs_candidates.csv , which identifies AGN candidates using central BPT diagnostics following Sánchez et al. (2018) , and a multi-wavelength compilation ( C AGN C_{\rm AGN} ) merging Comerford et al. (2020) 3 3 3 https://cdsarc.cds.unistra.fr/viz-bin/cat/J/ApJ/901/159 (406) and Comerford et al. (2024, 387) 4 4 4 https://data.sdss.org/sas/dr17/env/MANGA_AGN/v2_0_1/manga_agn-v2_0_1.fits . After cross-matching and removing duplicates, 249 unique AGN remain (77 S AGN S_{\rm AGN} ; 172 C AGN C_{\rm AGN} ; Table 2 ). To extend sensitivity to low radio luminosities, the MaNGA sample (9,828 galaxies) is cross-matched with the LoTSS DR2 catalogue 5 5 5 Low Frequency Array (LoFAR) Two-metre Sky Survey ( Shimwell et al. 2022 ) ( Hardcastle et al. 2023 , containing more than 4.0 million sources) 6 6 6 https://cdsarc.cds.unistra.fr/viz-bin/cat/J/A+A/678/A151 using a 5 ​ ″ 5\arcsec matching radius ( Mulcahey, C. R. et al. 2022 ) . Following Jin et al. (2025) , radio AGN fractions are normalised to the ∼ 5,500 \sim 5{,}500 MaNGA galaxies within the LoTSS footprint. Within this region, 2,436 galaxies ( ≈ 44.30 % \approx 44.30\% ) are detected at 144 MHz. Restricting to 2,252 galaxies with z < 0.1 z<0.1 minimises contamination from star formation ( Chilufya et al. 2024 ) . Selecting sources > 3 ​ σ >3\sigma above the L 144 L_{144} –SFR relation (appendix A.2 ) yields 261 radio AGN, reduced to 245 after applying our primary selection ( M ⋆ > 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{10}\,M_{\odot} , z < 0.085 z<0.085 ), and to 87 after removing duplicates. The final multi-wavelength catalogue therefore contains 386 unique AGN (Table 2 ; Fig. 1 ; Table 1 ). The classification traces distinct evolutionary stages: High excitation radio galaxies (HERGs) and broad-line AGN lie on or above the star-forming main sequence (MS), while low excitation radio galaxies (LERGs) and LoFAR-selected AGN are predominantly quiescent. At high stellar mass, a vertical gradient in accretion rate emerges along the SFR axis, with high-accretion systems in star-forming hosts and low-accretion systems in quenched galaxies. This agrees with Sabater et al. (2015) , supporting AGN activity regulated primarily by central cold gas supply, with the environment acting indirectly. sections.heading: 2.1.2 Galaxy environment and halo mass estimates
sections.text: Environmental classifications for the MaNGA sample are derived from the Yang et al. (2007) group catalogue, which utilises a halo-based group finder applied to SDSS galaxies ( Yang et al. 2005 ) . The algorithm identifies ∼ \sim 470,000 groups, providing central/satellite designations and halo mass ( M h M_{\rm h} ) estimates based on total stellar mass and R R -band luminosity. This methodology achieves ∼ \sim 80% accuracy in group membership and ∼ \sim 95% in central galaxy identification ( Marini et al. 2025a ) . For the ∼ \sim 30% of central galaxies without halo masses from the group catalogue; mainly isolated systems or those lacking members brighter than M R = − 19.5 M_{R}=-19.5 mag; we estimate M h M_{\rm h} using stellar–halo mass relations of Behroozi et al. (2013) ; Behroozi et al. (2019) . We test representativeness against SDSS in the same redshift range (complete to M ⋆ ∼ 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}\sim 10^{10}\,M_{\odot} ). Figure 2 shows good agreement: centrals dominate at all masses, increasing with M ⋆ M_{\star} , while satellites decline, confirming that MaNGA traces the underlying environmental demographics.

sections.heading: 2.2 The simulated dataset
sections.text: We evaluate the Magneticum, IllustrisTNG, and SIMBA suites to test their reproduction of the observed properties of hot halo gas and galaxy populations within dark matter halos, the multi-wavelength AGN activity trend on the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane, and the environmental effects on galaxy evolution. These simulations were selected according to their different ability in hot gas retention across three orders of magnitude of halo mass. According to Popesso, P. et al. (2026) , Magneticum currently shows the strongest alignment with eROSITA stacking results, followed by SIMBA, while IllustrisTNG exhibits larger discrepancies (see also appendix Fig. 9 ). To ensure consistency with MaNGA ( z < 0.085 z<0.085 , M ⋆ > 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{10}\,M_{\odot} ), we select simulated galaxies with M ⋆ > 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{10}\,M_{\odot} from z ≈ 0 z\approx 0 snapshots. The SFRs adopted for the simulated galaxies are the catalogue-provided instantaneous SFRs, computed from gas elements that are actively forming stars according to the adopted subgrid star-formation model. Prior to analysing quenching and the scaling relations between M ⋆ M_{\star} and M h M_{h} across different evolutionary phases, we validate the central–satellite demographics and the consistency between simulations and observations. As shown in Fig. 2 , the distributions show good statistical agreement across all datasets. sections.heading: 2.2.1 Magneticum
sections.text: We used two volumes of the Magneticum Pathfinder suite Dolag et al. (2025) to balance resolution with statistical power. Box4/uhr ( Teklu et al. 2015 ) (hereafter Box4) ( 48 ​ h − 1 ​ Mpc 48\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc} side) provides the resolution ( m gas = 7.3 × 10 6 ​ h − 1 ​ M ⊙ m_{\rm gas}=7.3\times 10^{6}\,h^{-1}\,M_{\odot} ) to resolve galaxies down to M ⋆ ≈ 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}\approx 10^{10}\,M_{\odot} ( Valenzuela et al. 2024 ) . Box2/hr (hereafter Box2) ( 352 ​ h − 1 ​ cMpc 352\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{cMpc} side) samples the massive halos necessary for f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} constraints. Both adopt a flat WMAP7 Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology ( Komatsu et al. 2011 ) and incorporate self-consistent SMBH growth and AGN feedback ( Hirschmann et al. 2014 ) . Magneticum successfully reproduces observed galaxy kinematics, angular momentum ( Valenzuela et al. 2024 ) , and hot gas fractions ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) . Crucially, both boxes match the central and satellite MaNGA distributions within 1 ​ σ 1\sigma (Fig. 2 ). For more details of the Magneticum Pathfinder, we refer the reader to 7 7 7 e.g., Dolag et al. (2015) , Remus et al. (2015) , Dolag (2019) , Biffi et al. (2022) , Valenzuela et al. (2024) , and Marini et al. (2025b) . This dual-box approach allows us to assess resolution effects while combining the detailed galaxy-scale information from Box4 with the statistical power of Box2. The larger volume of Box2 provides substantially improved sampling of rare massive galaxies ( M ⋆ > 10 11 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{11}\,M_{\odot} ). Nevertheless, the inferred central fractions differ by less than ∼ 10 % \sim 10\% between Box2 and Box4 across all stellar-mass bins, and by only ∼ 3 % \sim 3\% in the highest-mass bin (Fig. 2 ), indicating that the main trends are robust against volume-driven statistical fluctuations.

sections.heading: 2.2.2 IllustrisTNG (TNG100)
sections.text: For the IllustrisTNG suite ( Nelson et al. 2018 ; Springel et al. 2018 ; McDonough and Brainerd 2022 ) , we adopt the TNG100 volume ( ≈ 110 ​ Mpc \approx 110\,\mathrm{Mpc} comoving box). This intermediate size provides the optimal combination of volume and resolution ( m baryon = 2.1 × 10 6 ​ h − 1 ​ M ⊙ m_{\rm baryon}=2.1\times 10^{6}\,h^{-1}M_{\odot} ) to probe group-scale halos and compare directly with MaNGA demographics ( Lucie-Smith et al. 2024 ) . The simulation adopts a Planck 2015 Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology ( Planck Collaboration et al. 2016 ) . TNG100 incorporates magnetohydrodynamics and an updated subgrid physics suite, including stellar and AGN-driven feedback ( Weinberger et al. 2017 ; Pillepich et al. 2018b ) . As noted earlier, while TNG’s feedback prescriptions yield realistic star-forming fractions, they systematically overpredict hot gas masses in massive groups. This makes TNG100 a critical counterpoint to Magneticum for assessing the trade-off between halo gas retention and galaxy quenching.

sections.heading: 2.2.3 SIMBA
sections.text: The SIMBA cosmological simulation ( Davé et al. 2019 ) is evolved in a 100 ​ h − 1 ​ cMpc 100\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{cMpc} box, providing a balance between mass resolution ( m baryon ≃ 2.68 × 10 7 ​ h − 1 ​ M ⊙ m_{\rm baryon}\simeq 2.68\times 10^{7}\,h^{-1}\,M_{\odot} ) and cosmological representativeness comparable to TNG100 and Magneticum Box2/hr. SIMBA adopts a Planck 2015 cosmology ( Planck Collaboration et al. 2016 ) and utilises unique subgrid prescriptions for black hole growth, including torque-limited accretion for cold gas and Bondi accretion for hot gas ( Anglés-Alcázar et al. 2017 ; Davé et al. 2019 ) . In SIMBA, the kinetic jet mode is the primary driver for quenching in massive halos, efficiently heating the circumgalactic medium and suppressing accretion ( Katsianis et al. 2021 ; Scharré et al. 2024 ) . As highlighted earlier, SIMBA’s aggressive jet-driven feedback successfully matches observed gas fractions but typically results in an overabundance of quenched galaxies, making it an ideal candidate for exploring the physical coupling between halo-scale gas depletion and galaxy-scale overquenching.

sections.heading: 3 Galaxy populations in the SFR- M ⋆ M_{\star} plane
sections.text: In this section, we define the SFR- M ⋆ M_{\star} plane loci and use it to classify galaxy populations, which are finally studied by comparing both observation and simulations.

sections.heading: 3.1 Definition of the loci in the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane
sections.text: To characterise evolutionary pathways and the observed bimodality of the galaxy population ( Pović et al. 2013 ; Zhang et al. 2025 , e.g.,) , we define the star-forming main sequence (MS) as a reference for classifying galaxies according to their star formation activity. Given our focus on massive systems ( M ⋆ > 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{10}\,M_{\odot} ), we bypass the low-mass regime of log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≃ 9.75 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\simeq 9.75 where MaNGA volume-completeness corrections diverge as confirmed by Fraser-McKelvie and Cortese (2022) and adopt the log-linear parameterisation from Popesso et al. (2019b, Po19) defined by: log ⁡ ( SFR MS ) = ( 0.38 ± 0.04 ) ​ log ⁡ M ⋆ ​ [ M ⊙ ] − ( 3.83 ± 0.44 ) \log(\mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{MS}})=(0.38\pm 0.04)\,\log M_{\star}\,[M_{\odot}]-(3.83\pm 0.44) . This relation provides a better description of the high-mass MaNGA ridge than steeper relations such as Renzini and Peng (2015) and Belfiore et al. (2018) . Although more recent studies ( Popesso et al. 2023 , e.g.,) confirm the bending of the MS at high stellar masses, Po19 remains well suited to the local massive-galaxy regime explored here and captures the high-mass turnover that is central to our analysis. Our goal is to compare the full distribution of galaxies across the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane rather than simply separate star-forming and quiescent systems. Since the MS exhibits both a non-zero slope and a mass-dependent turnover, fixed sSFR thresholds can introduce stellar-mass-dependent classification biases, particularly at the massive end where the MS bends. We therefore classify galaxies relative to the MS, which removes the underlying stellar-mass dependence of star formation activity and provides a uniform framework for comparing observed and simulated populations across the full SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane. However, we note that our principal conclusions do not depend on this choice. As a robustness test, we repeated the analysis using a fixed threshold of log ⁡ ( sSFR / yr − 1 ) = − 11 \log(\mathrm{sSFR}/\mathrm{yr}^{-1})=-11 (Appendix A.3.1 and Fig. 11 ) and recovered the same qualitative ranking of the simulations. This demonstrates that the trends reported throughout this work are driven by genuine differences in galaxy populations rather than by the adopted classification scheme. By considering the Po19 MS, galaxies in both MaNGA and the simulations are classified according to their offset from the main sequence defined by: Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) = log ⁡ ( SFR gal ) − log ⁡ ( SFR MS ) \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR})=\log(\mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{gal}})-\log(\mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{MS}}) , where log ⁡ ( SFR MS ) \log(\mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{MS}}) is given by the Po19 MS relation, after rescaling all measurements to a common IMF. Following Bluck et al. (2020) , we define four distinct populations: • Highly star-forming galaxies i.e starbursts (SB): Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) > 0.6 \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR})>0.6 dex (pale yellow shaded region from the yellow vertical dashed line in Figure 3 ) • Star forming galaxies i.e in the main sequence (MS): − 0.3 < Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) < 0.6 -0.3<\Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR})<0.6 dex (region between yellow and pale green vertical dashed lines in Figure 3 ) • Transitional galaxies i.e green valley (GV): − 1.1 < Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) < − 0.3 -1.1<\Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR})<-0.3 dex (pale green shaded region between green and maroon vertical dashed lines in Figure 3 ) • Quiescent galaxies i.e galaxies in the red sequence (RS): Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) < − 1.1 \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR})<-1.1 dex (the pale red shaded region from the maroon vertical dashed lines in Figure 3 ) Figure 3: Comparison of MaNGA (solid curves) with simulations (dashed curves) in the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane, shown as the offset Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR}) [dex] from the Po19 main-sequence relation, for three stellar-mass bins: 10 10 10^{10} – 10 10.5 ​ M ⊙ 10^{10.5}\,M_{\odot} (blue curve), 10 10.5 10^{10.5} – 10 11 ​ M ⊙ 10^{11}\,M_{\odot} (green curve), and > 10 11 ​ M ⊙ >10^{11}\,M_{\odot} (purple curve). The top panels compare MaNGA with Magneticum (Box2 left, Box4 right), and the bottom panels compare MaNGA with SIMBA (left) and TNG100 (right). Vertical lines and shaded regions indicate the galaxy populations defined in Sect. 3.1 ; the RS, GV, MS, and SB labels shown in the top-left panel apply to all panels. Following Davé et al. (2019) ; Donnari et al. (2021) , simulated galaxies with SFR = 0 \mathrm{SFR}=0 are assigned random values drawn from a Gaussian centred at Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) ≈ − 3.0 \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR})\approx-3.0 dex for visualisation. The row order reflects decreasing agreement with the observed f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{h} relation (Appendix, Fig. 9 ), linking halo-scale gas depletion to galaxy-scale quenching. Magneticum best reproduces the observed f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{h} relation, followed by SIMBA, whereas TNG100 provides the closest match to the observed galaxy population in the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane. Figure 3 compares the Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR}) probability density functions (PDFs) of MaNGA and the three simulations in three stellar-mass bins: 10 10 10^{10} – 10 10.5 ​ M ⊙ 10^{10.5}\,M_{\odot} (blue curves), 10 10.5 10^{10.5} – 10 11 ​ M ⊙ 10^{11}\,M_{\odot} (green curves), and > 10 11 ​ M ⊙ >10^{11}\,M_{\odot} (purple curves). To accommodate finite numerical resolution in simulations and facilitate visualisation, galaxies with unresolved star formation ( SFR = 0 \mathrm{SFR}=0 in simulations) are assigned stochastic values with a Guassian distribution peaked around Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR}) = -3 dex from the MS and with a dispersion of 0.3 dex (more information, appendix B ). While their intrinsic distribution is physically unconstrained, these galaxies would reside significantly below the MS, effectively populating the quenched region ( Donnari et al. 2019 ) .

sections.heading: 3.2 Observed versus simulated SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane
sections.text: Direct comparisons between observations and simulations are subject to survey volume, selection effects, and mass-dependent sampling. To mitigate these biases, galaxies are binned in stellar mass (0.5 dex), and we focus on relative distribution shapes rather than absolute normalizations. We analyse the PDF of the offset from the main sequence, where Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) = 0 \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR})=0 corresponds to the Po19 relation. As shown in Fig. 3 , the MaNGA MS distribution closely follows the Po19 relation, with a typical dispersion of ≈ 0.3 \approx 0.3 dex. Toward higher stellar masses, an increasing fraction of galaxies populates the GV and RS. A pronounced accumulation at Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) ≈ − 1.5 \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR})\approx-1.5 , just below the GV region, likely reflects a physical or instrumental floor rather than residual star formation (see details, appendix B ). One of the debates on this apparent “quiescent peak” is that it can be attributed to systematic uncertainties in SFR diagnostics. Infrared tracers may be contaminated by dust heated by old stellar populations ( Kouroumpatzakis et al. 2023 ) , while UV indicators are affected by emission from evolved stars (e.g., post-AGB and horizontal branch; Salim et al. 2007 ; Salim et al. 2016 ). In addition, SED fitting and D ​ 4000 D4000 diagnostics suffer from age–metallicity degeneracies and priors that disfavor zero-SFR solutions ( van de Sande et al. 2015 ; Borghi et al. 2022 ) . Together, these effects indicate that the observed quiescent peak primarily reflects methodological limitations rather than ongoing star formation. However, throughout this study, we concur with Donnari et al. (2019) that these galaxies are attributed to the quiescent region, and we count them as detailed above.

sections.heading: 3.2.1 MaNGA versus Magneticum
sections.text: Magneticum provides the closest match to the observed hot gas fractions among the simulations considered (Fig. 9 ). However, it performs poorly in reproducing the galaxy population, (Fig. 3 ). The location of the MS is consistent with observations only in the lowest stellar-mass bin ( 10 10.0 10^{10.0} – 10 10.5 ​ M ⊙ 10^{10.5}\,M_{\odot} ) when using the lower-resolution Box2 run. No clear green valley (GV) is present: instead, Magneticum produces a single log-normal distribution with a pronounced tail toward SFR=0. This tail hosts a substantial quenched population, highlighted by the artificial Gaussian component placed at Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) = − 3 \Delta\log({\rm SFR})=-3 . The resulting overquenching is most severe in the higher stellar-mass bins, where the MS becomes almost indistinguishable. The comparison with the higher-resolution Box4 run shows a similar overall behaviour. Although Box4 recovers a more visible MS at higher stellar masses-suggesting some resolution dependence-the level of quenching remains excessive (see Table 3 ), with the majority of galaxies still populating the low-SFR tail below the MS. A distinct GV is still absent. Moreover, although MaNGA galaxies at high masses are predominantly quenched, Box4 exhibits an excess of star-forming systems, including in the starburst region (see also Table 3 ). The persistence of overquenching across different resolutions indicates that this behaviour is driven by the subgrid physics ( Rihtaršič et al. 2024 ) , rather than by numerical resolution or volume effects. Magneticum systematically overpredicts the quenched fraction, suggesting that its AGN feedback is too efficient at removing or heating the gas, thereby suppressing star formation and preventing galaxy rejuvenation. As a result, the simulated galaxy population is significantly more quenched than observed in the local Universe.

sections.heading: 3.2.2 MaNGA versus SIMBA
sections.text: SIMBA is the second-best performer in reproducing the observed hot gas fractions (Fig. 9 ). However, the comparison of the Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) \Delta\log({\rm SFR}) distributions reveals significant discrepancies with respect to the observed galaxy population (Fig. 3 ). While SIMBA broadly recovers the location of the MS, the observed MaNGA MS is significantly narrower and more sharply defined, particularly in the 10 10.0 10^{10.0} – 10 10.5 ​ M ⊙ 10^{10.5}\,M_{\odot} bin. As in Magneticum (Box4), SIMBA exhibits strong overquenching across all stellar masses. Even in the lowest mass bin, only ∼ 23 % \sim 23\% of galaxies lie on the MS, in stark contrast with the majority of MaNGA galaxies (see Table 3 ). This behaviour is likely driven by the high efficiency of AGN-driven winds and X-ray feedback ( Davé et al. 2019 ; Scharré et al. 2024 ) . Unlike Magneticum, SIMBA reproduces the bimodal distribution of galaxies, with a well-defined green valley, particularly at M ⋆ < 10 11 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}<10^{11}\,M_{\odot} . Nevertheless, most galaxies are still concentrated in the low-SFR tail, as indicated by the prominent peak of the artificial Gaussian distribution at Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) = − 3 \Delta\log({\rm SFR})=-3 . We also confirm previous findings of elevated SFRs and a higher incidence of starburst galaxies at low-to-intermediate stellar masses ( Rodighiero et al. 2011 ; Davé et al. 2019 ) . Generally, SIMBA reproduces the main sequence, bimodality, and mass-dependent quenching, but still overquenches galaxies less than Magneticum, yet more than observed.

sections.heading: 3.2.3 MaNGA versus TNG100
sections.text: IllustrisTNG exhibits the largest discrepancy with the observed hot gas fractions (Fig. 9 ). However, it provides the best agreement with the observed galaxy population among the simulations considered (Fig. 3 ). Across all stellar mass bins, TNG100 reproduces the MS in good agreement with MaNGA, although it slightly overpredicts the fraction of starburst galaxies ( ∼ 1.36 % \sim 1.36\% , Table 3 ), possibly due to the larger hot gas reservoir available for star formation. As in Magneticum, IllustrisTNG does not show a clearly defined green valley, instead displaying a continuous distribution with a tail toward SFR=0. Despite this, it achieves the closest match to the observed galaxy distribution, particularly in reproducing both the MS and the quiescent population (Table 3 . A notable discrepancy appears only in the highest stellar mass bin, where an excess of star-forming galaxies suggests that quenching in massive systems is less efficient than observed ( Genel et al. 2018 ; Cannarozzo et al. 2023 ) . Tests using the larger-volume IllustrisTNG300 simulation yield consistent results, indicating that these trends are not driven by resolution effects. IllustrisTNG’s weak AGN feedback reproduces the main sequence and a substantial fraction of the quiescent population, consistent with previous studies showing reasonable agreement with observed quenched fractions ( Donnari et al. 2019 ) . However, in our classification scheme, the excess of star-forming galaxies in the highest stellar-mass bin suggests that quenching in the most massive systems is somewhat less efficient than observed, potentially due to the retention of hot halo gas. Overall, simulations face a key tension: matching CGM thermodynamics leads to overquenching of star formation, while matching galaxy properties fails to remove sufficient gas from the halo.

sections.heading: 4 AGN distribution in the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane
sections.text: AGN feedback has long been proposed as a primary mechanism regulating galaxy evolution, suppressing star formation by heating or ejecting gas from the host ( Pović et al. 2012 ; Sánchez et al. 2018 ) . In cosmological simulations, this feedback is essential for quenching massive galaxies and shaping black hole-host correlations Weinberger et al. (2017) . However, the location of AGN hosts relative to the star-forming main sequence remains debated ( Lammers et al. 2023 ) , likely due to the episodic nature of accretion and selection biases ( Sánchez et al. 2018 ) . From left, the first two panels are for Magneticum (Box2 and Box4, respectively), SIMBA (third panel), and TNG100 (fourth panel). sections.heading: 4.1 Observation: Accretion gradients traced by SFR
sections.text: According to Fig. 1 (see also table 1 ), The SFR-stellar mass plane reflects a transition in accretion mode, with declining SFR marking the shift from radiatively efficient to jet-dominated, inefficient feedback, as previously suggested by Best and Heckman (2012a) . This is because most AGN appear regulated by cold gas supply via secular processes ( Sabater et al. 2015 ) . The radiatively efficient populations - HERGs, broad-line, X-ray, MIR, and optical AGN - predominantly occupy the star-forming regime. HERGs ( Δ ​ SFR ≈ + 0.18 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 \Delta\mathrm{SFR}\approx+0.18\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1} ) trace gas-rich mergers driving high-Eddington accretion and starburst activity ( Best and Heckman 2012a ) . Elevated SFRs in X-ray AGN support this connection, consistent with FIR studies ( Mahoro et al. 2017 ; Mahoro et al. 2019 ; Mahoro et al. 2023 ) . Broad-line ( Δ ​ SFR ≈ + 0.07 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 \Delta\mathrm{SFR}\approx+0.07\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1} ) and Swift/BAT X-ray AGN ( Δ ​ SFR ≈ − 0.01 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 \Delta\mathrm{SFR}\approx-0.01\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1} ) cluster near the MS, although a few X-ray sources extend below the MS, consistent with Igo et al. (2024) based on eFEDS and LOFAR data. Optically selected AGN span a broader evolutionary range (median Δ ​ SFR ≈ − 0.36 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 \Delta\mathrm{SFR}\approx-0.36\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1} ), tracing the transition from the MS to the RS ( Ellison et al. 2016 ) . While GV occupancy depends on selection ( Sánchez et al. 2018 ; Nyiransengiyumva et al. 2026 ) , our results indicate that radiatively efficient accretion persists into the GV, consistent with feedback models in which AGN suppress central star formation over Gyr timescales prior to global quenching ( Hickox et al. 2009 ; Sánchez et al. 2018 ; Lammers et al. 2023 ) . Conversely, LERGs ( log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≈ 11.47 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\approx 11.47 , Δ ​ SFR ≈ − 1.16 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 \Delta\mathrm{SFR}\approx-1.16\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1} ) and LoFAR-selected AGN ( log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≈ 11.29 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\approx 11.29 , Δ ​ SFR ≈ − 1.38 ​ M ⊙ ​ yr − 1 \Delta\mathrm{SFR}\approx-1.38\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1} ) trace the endpoint of galaxy evolution. They lie > 1 >1 dex below the MS and are confined to massive ( log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) > 11.3 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})>11.3 ), quenched hosts ( Igo and Merloni 2025 ; Jin et al. 2025 ) with old stellar populations ( Kauffmann et al. 2004 ) , indicating a tight connection between radio-mode activity and sustained quenching ( Comerford et al. 2020 ) . Jin et al. (2025) show that quenching occurred ≈ 5 \approx 5 Gyr prior to the observed radio phase, implying that jets provide preventative rather than causative feedback. In these systems, kinetic energy dominates the energy budget, offsetting halo cooling and maintaining quiescence ( Igo and Merloni 2025 , maintenance mode;) . Overall (Fig. 1 ), a clear trend emerges at M ⋆ ≈ 10 11 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}\approx 10^{11}\,M_{\odot} : high-accretion AGN lie on or above the main sequence, while low-accretion systems cluster in the quenched regime, producing a strong vertical gradient in accretion rate along the SFR axis. This supports a framework in which AGN activity is primarily governed by central cold gas supply, with environmental effects acting indirectly ( Sabater et al. 2015 ) .

sections.heading: 4.2 Simulations: Accretion gradients driven by stellar mass
sections.text: We assess whether cosmological simulations reproduce the observed AGN trends in the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane. Black holes (BHs) are modeled as collisionless sink particles that grow via gas accretion and mergers ( Sijacki et al. 2007 ; Hirschmann et al. 2014 ) , with feedback implemented through subgrid prescriptions that couple accretion energy to the surrounding gas, regulating both BH growth and host evolution ( Somerville and Davé 2015 ) . As simulations lack synthetic spectra or broadband luminosities, we use the specific BH accretion rate as a proxy for AGN activity: λ BHAR = log ⁡ ( BHAR M BH ) ​ [ yr − 1 ] \lambda_{\rm BHAR}=\log\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{BHAR}}{M_{\rm BH}}\right)\,[\mathrm{yr}^{-1}] , where BHAR is the accretion rate and M BH M_{\rm BH} the BH mass. High λ BHAR \lambda_{\rm BHAR} indicates radiatively efficient growth, while low values correspond to maintenance-mode systems. To reduce the influence of poorly resolved low- M BH M_{\rm BH} , we limit the analysis to 10 6 ≤ M BH / M ⊙ ≤ 10 8.5 10^{6}\leq M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot}\leq 10^{8.5} .

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Qualitative agreements: Mass-dependent quenching
sections.text: In Fig. 4 , all models show a strong dependence of λ BHAR \lambda_{\rm BHAR} on stellar mass ( M ⋆ M_{\star} ), with high accretion rates ( λ BHAR > − 10.5 ​ yr − 1 \lambda_{\rm BHAR}>-10.5\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1} ) concentrated in low-mass galaxies, reflecting high gas fractions, though often indicating over-cooling prior to BH seeding ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) . Intermediate accretion ( − 11.5 ≲ λ BHAR ​ ( yr − 1 ) ≲ − 10.5 -11.5\lesssim\lambda_{\rm BHAR}\,(\mathrm{yr}^{-1})\lesssim-10.5 ) traces systems crossing the green valley. At M ⋆ > 10 11 , M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{11},M_{\odot} , galaxies are dominated by low accretion ( λ BHAR < − 11.5 , yr − 1 \lambda_{\rm BHAR}<-11.5,{\rm yr}^{-1} ), consistent with quenched systems. The more gradual decline observed in SIMBA suggests that efficient quenching does not require an abrupt shutdown of black-hole growth. This behaviour is consistent with SIMBA’s two-mode accretion and feedback model, in which jet-mode feedback efficiently suppresses star formation while low-level black-hole accretion persists ( Davé et al. 2019 ) , consistent with the broader distribution of low-to-intermediate accretion states observed in our SIMBA sample. Although SIMBA shows a more gradual decline, all models primarily regulate BH growth with M ⋆ M_{\star} rather than SFR.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Systematic mismatches: The role of gas supply
sections.text: A key discrepancy arises between observations and simulations. MaNGA links black hole accretion to the instantaneous cold-gas supply traced by SFR, whereas simulations regulate AGN primarily via host mass. Consequently, models underpredict high-accretion AGN in massive star-forming galaxies, reflecting radio-mode feedback tied to the most massive systems ( Somerville and Davé 2015 , see review) . Simulations thus exhibit a dual mismatch: they underpredict high-accretion AGN in massive star-forming galaxies and fail to decouple radio-mode activity from residual star formation in quenched systems. sections.heading: 5 Environmental role in quenching
sections.text: To evaluate environmental dependencies in both datasets, we examine: (i) the centrals and satellites distribution across the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane, and (ii) galaxy fraction variations across SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} loci as a function of host halo mass. In Figure 5 , consistent with (e.g., Popesso et al. 2019a ; de Isídio et al. 2026 , as observed in the SDSS sample) , centrals dominate the MS and high-mass regimes, while satellites are at low-mass ( M ⋆ < 10 10.5 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}<10^{10.5}\,M_{\odot} ) preferentially populating the quiescent region. In simulations, central and satellite populations are identified via Friends-of-Friends (FoF) and Subfind algorithms ( Springel et al. 2001 ; Dolag et al. 2009 ) , defining the most massive subhalo as the central and the rest are satellites ( Mun et al. 2025 , e.g.,) . Rather than isolating specific physical mechanisms, we only assess whether cumulative environmental prescriptions in Magneticum, IllustrisTNG, and SIMBA reproduce the central-satellite demographics observed in MaNGA. sections.heading: 5.1 Stellar mass dependencies for centrals and satellites
sections.text: Figure 6 shows the fractions of centrals (top row) and satellites (bottom row) as a function of stellar mass across regions of the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane for MaNGA (solid) and simulations (dashed). In all datasets the MS fraction declines and the RS fraction increases with stellar mass, consistent with mass-quenching trends ( Peng et al. 2010 , e.g.,) . Differences in the GV population reflect the non detection of the GV in simulations and the variations in quenching timescales.

sections.heading: 5.1.1 Central galaxies
sections.text: MaNGA centrals show a gradual transition from MS-dominated systems at log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ∼ 10 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\sim 10 to RS dominance only above log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ∼ 11.5 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\sim 11.5 , with a substantial GV population at intermediate masses. In Magneticum instead RS fractions dominate by log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ∼ 10.5 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\sim 10.5 , while the GV component is strongly suppressed, indicating short transition timescales likely driven by efficient AGN feedback. Retaining residual star formation at intermediate masses may improve agreement with observations ( Katsianis et al. 2021 , e.g.,) . SIMBA shows a similar early transition, with RS fractions exceeding the MS at log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≈ 10.5 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\approx 10.5 and with a nearly complete quenched population at log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≈ 11.5 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\approx 11.5 . The weak GV population and the negligible SB component are consistent with rapid quenching driven by kinetic AGN feedback and hot-gas suppression of star formation ( Davé et al. 2019 ; Gabor and Davé 2015 , e.g.,) . IllustrisTNG100 shows the most gradual transition among the simulations. The RS fraction overtakes MS at log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ∼ 10.75 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\sim 10.75 –11.0, still earlier than MaNGA but significantly later than Magneticum or SIMBA. The GV population remains present at intermediate masses, partially overlapping with MaNGA uncertainty bands. For high mass centrals, AGN feedback associated with SMBH growth is likely the dominant internal quenching channel, as suggested by Donnari et al. (2021) . SB galaxies remain subdominant. This suggests more realistic quenching timescales, in agreement with previous IllustrisTNG analyses ( Genel et al. 2018 , e.g.,) .

sections.heading: 5.1.2 Satellite galaxies
sections.text: MaNGA satellites are more quenched than centrals at fixed stellar mass but still show a gradual transition with a visible GV population. In Magneticum, satellites are strongly overquenched. RS fractions reach ∼ 0.7 \sim 0.7 –0.9 by log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≈ 10.5 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\approx 10.5 and approach unity near log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot}) ≈ \approx 11, while MS and GV populations nearly vanish. This behaviour is consistent with efficient environmental quenching by hot halo gas ( Gabor and Davé 2015 , e.g.,) . In SIMBA, satellites show a similar trend, with RS fractions increasing from ∼ 0.7 \sim 0.7 at log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≈ 10.25 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\approx 10.25 and approaching unity toward the highest masses. The GV population remains small and SB galaxies are negligible, indicating strong preventative feedback ( Davé et al. 2019 ) . IllustrisTNG100 exhibits the mildest satellite quenching. MS fractions remain significant over log ⁡ ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≈ 10.25 \log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\approx 10.25 –11.25 and a visible GV component persists at intermediate masses. Although quenched satellites are still somewhat overpredicted at the highest masses, IllustrisTNG100 qualitatively reproduces well the observed pattern of MS, GV, RS and slightly the SB compared to other simulations. Based on our M ⋆ > 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{10}\,M_{\odot} data, the quenched pattern is consistent with results obtained by Donnari et al. (2021) using the IllustrisTNG100 and SDSS data at z = 0 z=0 . In summary, simulations broadly reproduce the mass dependence of satellite quenching but differ in strength: Magneticum and SIMBA overpredict quenched satellites, while IllustrisTNG100 provides the closest match to the MaNGA trends.

sections.heading: 5.2 Halo mass dependencies
sections.text: Galaxy–halo scaling relations reveal a strong connection between stellar mass and dark matter halo properties ( Toptun et al. 2026 , e.g.,) . Although these relations are observationally robust, the physical origin of their scatter remains uncertain and continues to challenge galaxy formation models ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) . To evaluate the consistency between observations and simulations, we perform two diagnostics. First, we examine the stellar-to-halo mass relation ( M c ​ e ​ n ​ t / M h M_{cent}/M_{h} versus M h M_{h} , hereafter, SHMR). Since environmental processes are primarily governed by the total halo mass of the host potential well in which satellites reside ( Behroozi et al. 2013 ; Moster et al. 2010 ; Donnari et al. 2021 ) , we consider only central galaxies. The SHMR traces the efficiency of baryon-to-star conversion, which peaks near M h ∼ 10 12 M_{h}\sim 10^{12} – 10 12.5 ​ M ⊙ 10^{12.5}\,M_{\odot} and declines toward higher halo masses ( Behroozi et al. 2013 ; Birrer et al. 2014 ; Lu et al. 2015 ; Rodríguez-Puebla et al. 2017 ; Behroozi et al. 2019 ) . Our analysis focuses on the high-mass regime beyond this peak, where AGN feedback becomes the dominant quenching mechanism ( Kravtsov et al. 2018 ; Erfanianfar et al. 2019 ; Golden-Marx et al. 2022 ) . Second, we analyse the satellite fraction across the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane as a function of halo mass. These test provides a direct test of whether feedback and environmental processes prescriptions in hydrodynamical simulations reproduce the stellar content of group halos.

sections.heading: 5.2.1 The stellar-to-halo mass relation
sections.text: Figure 7: The stellar-to-halo mass relation ( M ⋆ / M h M_{\star}/M_{h} vs. M h M_{h} ) for MaNGA (first), Magneticum Box2 and Box4 (second and third, respectively), SIMBA (fourth) and IllustrisTNG (fifth). Points are color-coded by log ⁡ ( sSFR ) \log(\mathrm{sSFR}) . Lines show semi-empirical models from Moster et al. (2010) (magenta), Moster et al. (2018) (yellow), and Moster et al. (2013) (cyan). White points and black curves indicate the median trend. Figure 8: Satellite fractions in the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane as a function of halo mass. Galaxy loci are defined relative to the Po19 main sequence: SB (magenta), MS (blue), GV (green), and RS (red). Solid lines show MaNGA measurements and dashed lines show simulation predictions. Figure 7 shows the SHMR across observations and simulations. Consistent with previous studies ( Moster et al. 2010 ; Moster et al. 2013 ; Behroozi et al. 2013 ; Moster et al. 2018 ; Behroozi et al. 2019 ; de Isídio et al. 2024 ; Toptun et al. 2026 , e.g.,) , the observational data and simulations are broadly consistent with a peak near M h ≈ 10 12 M_{\rm h}\approx 10^{12} – 10 12.5 ​ M ⊙ 10^{12.5}\,M_{\odot} , where the SHMR reaches its maximum ( Behroozi et al. 2013 ) . While this feature is less pronounced in Magneticum, particularly Box2, tests including lower-mass haloes indicate that the peak becomes more evident once the stellar-mass selection is relaxed, suggesting that the weaker feature is primarily driven by the adopted sample selection. At higher masses, the relation declines, reflecting the transition from cold gas accretion to hot, virialized halo atmospheres that suppress fresh gas inflow ( Popesso et al. 2019a ) . Our sample is intentionally restricted to M ⋆ > 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{10}\,M_{\odot} , corresponding to the regime where AGN feedback is expected to dominate over stellar feedback and where the tension between reproducing halo gas fractions and galaxy populations is most pronounced. In this regime, stellar mass growth is increasingly dominated by AGN feedback and ex-situ assembly ( Toptun et al. 2026 , e.g.,) . The MaNGA (first panel) SHMR shows mild deviations from semi-empirical models of Moster et al. (2010) ; Moster et al. (2013) ; Moster et al. (2018) . This likely reflects the limited volume of the MaNGA sample, which underrepresents the most massive brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs). Nevertheless, the median trend remains broadly consistent with Moster et al. (2010) . The scatter does not correlate with log(sSFR) and likely reflects uncertainties in halo mass estimates from the Yang et al. (2007) group catalogue. Magneticum (second and third panels) displays larger differences between the two simulation boxes: Box4 broadly agrees with IllustrisTNG100, whereas Box2 produces a flatter SHMR. The concentration of star-forming galaxies in lower-mass halos in Box2 may result from selection effects or from inefficient early stellar feedback that allows excessive gas cooling ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) . At higher halo masses, continued star formation suggests that AGN feedback may not fully suppress cooling flows. SIMBA (fourth panel) shows a tighter correlation at low halo masses but produces a lower median SHMR than observed. IllustrisTNG (fifth panel) shows good agreement with both MaNGA and semi-empirical models, although the simulated relation is slightly flatter. Across all simulations, the absence of a strong log(sSFR) dependence in the scatter suggests that local CGM thermodynamic conditions regulate star formation more directly than halo mass alone.

sections.heading: 5.2.2 The role of M h M_{h} on satellites in the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane
sections.text: Figure 8 shows the satellite fractions across the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane versus M h M_{h} . Compared to simulations, MaNGA satellites display a more gradual dependence on M h M_{h} , with fractions nearly constant across the M h M_{h} range. With the exclusion of the lowest halo mass bin at M h < 10 12.5 ​ M ⊙ M_{h}<10^{12.5}\,M_{\odot} , Magneticum Box2 and Box4 consistently show a significant overquenching of satellites with 60-80% of them in the RS. The same is true for SIMBA. In contrast, IllustrisTNG100 shows milder quenching, with MS satellites decreasing from (80–40) % \% at M h < 10 13 . ​ M ⊙ M_{h}<10^{13.}\,M_{\odot} , to 20% in the cluster halo regime, where galaxies tend to be more in the RS, consistent with Donnari et al. (2021) . Overall, while most simulations over-quench satellites, IllustrisTNG100 better reproduces MaNGA trends, whereas SIMBA captures GV systems but quenches satellites earlier than observed. Despite these differences, all simulations highlight the strong role of the halo mass in satellite quenching, supporting the importance of halo virialization and environmental processes ( Gabor and Davé 2015 , e.g.,) . The qualitative similar quenched fractions in Box2 and Box4 further suggest sensitivity to subgrid feedback prescriptions.

sections.heading: 6 Summary and conclusions
sections.text: This study evaluates whether current feedback frameworks: IllustrisTNG ( Nelson et al. 2018 ; Springel et al. 2018 ) , Magneticum ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) , and SIMBA ( Davé et al. 2019 ) can simultaneously reproduce the observed hot-halo gas properties and galaxy demographics. Our comparison with MaNGA reveals a consistent trade-off: • The Magneticum suite (Box2/Box4) effectively matches eROSITA-derived hot gas fractions ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) . However, this successful gas expulsion comes at the cost of severe over-quenching (RS > 93 % >93\% ), causing galaxies to bypass the GV transition phase too rapidly and distorting the observed SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane. • SIMBA employs jet-dominated feedback ( Davé et al. 2019 ) to achieve halo gas depletion. While it moderately reproduces gaseous observations, quenching is triggered prematurely at M ⋆ < 10 10.5 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}<10^{10.5}\,M_{\odot} , leading to a faster-than-observed migration toward the RS. • IllustrisTNG100, calibrated primarily on galaxy statistics such as the stellar mass function and morphology ( Nelson et al. 2018 ; Springel et al. 2018 ) , faithfully reproduces MS slopes and observed quenched fractions (e.g., matching the 28 % 28\% GV fraction). Nevertheless, it lacks sufficient energetic feedback to match eROSITA measurements, retaining too much hot gas in group and cluster-scale halos and maintaining an excess of MS galaxies in all stellar mass bins. We also identify a fundamental mismatch in AGN triggering: MaNGA shows a vertical accretion-rate gradient (SFR-driven), while simulations produce a horizontal gradient (stellar mass-driven), tying black hole growth to host stellar mass rather than star-forming state and availability of gas to fuel the accreation process. Overall, no current simulation simultaneously reproduces both detailed galaxy demographics and hot-halo gas properties, underscoring the persistent tension between matching stellar and gaseous observables. Achieving a self-consistent model therefore requires feedback that regulates star formation while simultaneously controlling the thermodynamic state of the circum- and intra-galactic medium, something missing in current model prescriptions. As a way forward, in a companion paper (Paper II) we will test these conclusions using the FLAMINGO fiducial and extreme f gas − 8 ​ σ f_{\rm gas}-8\sigma models, investigating whether the feedback strength required to match halo gas constraints necessarily results in overquenched or otherwise distorted galaxy populations. sections.heading: A.3.1 Robustness to the adopted galaxy-classification scheme
sections.text: To test the sensitivity of our results to the classification adopted in Section 3.1 (i.e Po19-based Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR}) ), we repeated the analysis using a fixed threshold of log ⁡ ( sSFR / yr − 1 ) = − 11 \log(\mathrm{sSFR}/\mathrm{yr}^{-1})=-11 (see Fig. 11 ). Although this method does not trace the entire SFR- M ⋆ M_{\star} plane, it helps to assess the overall trend of star formation. Comparing the Po19-based Δ ​ log ⁡ ( SFR ) \Delta\log(\mathrm{SFR}) (Fig. 3 , Table. 3 ) and sSFR (Fig. 11 ) classifications yields a 10–20% difference in quenched fractions at low stellar masses due to the green-valley population, but <5% at higher masses. Crucially, the simulation ranking is unchanged: Magneticum shows the strongest quenching, followed by SIMBA and TNG100, confirming the robustness of our results. sections.heading: Appendix B Galaxy star-formation activity classification
sections.text: As pointed by Donnari et al. (2019) , the distinction between ’quenched’ and ’star-forming’ galaxies is inherently ambiguous and arbitrary. Both simulations and observations lack a non-arbitrary zero-point, as quenching typically represents either a numerical resolution limit or the sensitivity floor of star-formation tracers. The uncertainties and biases in the SFR measurements can create the appearance of a bimodal distribution ( Feldmann 2017 ) . Therefore, in SFR- M ⋆ M_{\star} plane, the terms bimodality, green valley and red sequence work as long as we count galaxies with unresolved/undetectable SFR (assigned zero SFR in simulations) and log(sSFR) < 10 − 12 ​ yr − 1 <10^{-12}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1} in observations, otherwise Feldmann (2017) ; Eales et al. (2018) the logarithmic distribution of SFR is unimodal forming a peak at the star-forming sequence and an extended tail towards low SFRs.

Received 13 April 2026 / Accepted 13 July 2026 Abstract Aims. Accurately balancing gas reservoirs, star formation, and feedback processes across cosmic time remains one of the central challenges for galaxy formation models implemented in modern hydrodynamical simulations. While different feedback prescriptions can reproduce selected local galaxy properties with varying success, some of the most pronounced discrepancies emerge when comparing predictions for the hot gas content of dark matter halos. Methods. In this study, we examine three state-of-the-art cosmological simulations: Magneticum, IllustrisTNG, and SIMBA, which struggle to simultaneously reproduce the observed galaxy and halo gas properties in the local Universe. We confront their predictions with spatially resolved galaxy data from MaNGA and recent observational constraints on the hot gas mass fraction–halo mass ( f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{\mathrm{h}} ) relation derived from eROSITA and Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (SZ) measurements. Results. Reproducing the observed relation f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{\mathrm{h}} requires strong active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback. However, such strong feedback often leads to excessive quenching in simulated galaxy populations. Magneticum and SIMBA successfully match the observed gas fraction relation but predict an overabundance of quenched galaxies. In contrast, IllustrisTNG implements comparatively weaker AGN feedback, yielding more realistic star-forming fractions but systematically overpredicting hot gas masses in massive groups and poor clusters. Conclusions. In general, the stated tensions indicate that the current feedback models remain incomplete, not only in terms of the total energy injected but also in terms of the timing, location and coupling of this energy to the surrounding gas. Our results, therefore, highlight the need to revisit subgrid feedback prescriptions and to develop more self-consistent models capable of simultaneously regulating galaxy growth and the thermodynamic properties of halo gas. Motivated by this discrepancy, a companion study will explore whether the feedback strengths required to match halo gas constraints inevitably lead to overquenching and distorted galaxy demographics. Key Words. galaxies: evolution – galaxies: active – galaxies: halos – galaxies: clusters: general – cosmology: theory – methods: numerical 1 Introduction Understanding how galaxies and their host halos co-evolve requires a consistent picture of the baryonic cycle across a wide mass range, from Milky Way–sized halos to massive clusters. It is well established that low-mass halos predominantly host star-forming galaxies, while massive halos tend to host quenched systems. This trend suggests that star formation is regulated by a transition from stellar feedback-dominated processes at low masses to AGN-driven quenching at high masses ( Dekel and Silk 1986 ; Kauffmann et al. 2004 ; Hopkins et al. 2012 , e.g.,) . In the galaxy group mass range (i.e. ≈ 10 13 − 14 ​ M ⊙ \approx 10^{13-14}M_{\odot} ), classical models predicted that galaxy groups retain a large fraction of their baryons in the hot intragroup medium (IGrM). In contrast, recent observational studies including X-ray measurements from eROSITA reveal that galaxy groups with halo masses 10 12 − 14 ​ M ⊙ 10^{12-14}M_{\odot} are strongly depleted in hot gas relative to the cosmic baryon fraction ( Zhang et al. 2025 ; Popesso, P. et al. 2026 ) . These systems retain only ≈ ( 20 CLOSE \approx(20 – OPEN 40 ) % 40)\% of the expected baryons within R 200 R_{200} 1 1 1 R 200 R_{200} the radius enclosing a mean density 200 times the critical density of the Universe. , implying that feedback processes redistribute baryons far beyond the virial region. Independent constraints from the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel’dovich (kSZ) effect also indicate that halo gas profiles are significantly more extended than predicted by standard models ( Hadzhiyska et al. 2025 ; Bigwood et al. 2026 ; Siegel et al. 2026 ) . In particular, Siegel et al. (2026) combine X-ray gas fractions with kSZ measurements over 13 < log 10 ⁡ ( M 500 / M ⊙ ) < 14 13<\log_{10}(M_{500}/M_{\odot})<14 and infer that strong feedback suppresses the matter power spectrum by ≈ 10 ± 2 % \approx 10\pm 2\% at k = 1 ​ h ​ Mpc − 1 k=1\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc^{-1}} , consistent with baryons being displaced to large radii. Additional support for extended baryon reservoirs comes from fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures, which probe the integrated electron column density along extragalactic sightlines ( Lanman et al. 2026 ) . Despite these observational indications of strong baryon redistribution, cosmological hydrodynamical simulations often struggle to reproduce the low gas fractions inferred for galaxy groups. Most models rely on subgrid prescriptions for black hole accretion and AGN feedback that operate below the resolution scale, introducing uncertainties in the predicted thermodynamic structure of halo gas ( Puchwein and Springel 2013 ; Weinberger et al. 2017 ; Schulze et al. 2018 ) . Moreover, simulations are typically calibrated to match the galaxy stellar mass function ( Vogelsberger et al. 2014 ; Schaye et al. 2015 ) , while hot-gas properties are often tuned using X-ray–selected samples biassed toward gas-rich systems ( McCarthy et al. 2010 ; McCarthy et al. 2017 ; Schaye and others 2023 ) . Such samples exclude the X-ray-faint populations identified in volume-limited eROSITA surveys ( Marini et al. 2024 ; Popesso et al. 2025 ) , leading many simulations to overpredict the hot gas content of group-scale halos despite reproducing galaxy statistics near the Milky-Way mass scale ( Shreeram et al. 2025 ) . Among current simulation suites, the Magneticum simulations provide an alternative approach. Their feedback parameters are chosen to reproduce cluster scaling relations and the Magorrian relation rather than explicitly tuning the stellar mass function ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) . Nevertheless, Magneticum has been shown to reproduce several key observed galaxy properties, including the stellar mass function over a broad stellar-mass range, the mass–metallicity relation, and the cosmic star-formation history ( Dolag et al. 2025 ) . Furthermore, Magneticum reproduces several hot-gas observables, including gas fractions and luminosity–mass relations, in close agreement with eROSITA measurements ( Dolag et al. 2016 ; Dolag et al. 2025 ; Toptun et al. 2025 ; Popesso, P. et al. 2026 ) . A key goal of this work is to assess whether this success also extends to reproducing the observed distribution of galaxy populations in the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane, their AGN activity, and their environmental dependence. This issue is closely tied to the co-evolution of AGN and their host galaxies. The hot gas constitutes the dominant baryonic reservoir in massive halos, and its cooling within the circum-galactic region can provide a sustained fuel supply for star formation. This process is particularly important in galaxy groups and clusters, where gas accretion occurs predominantly in the hot mode. In this regime, central galaxies are no longer fed by cold gas streams from cosmic web filaments, as these are unable to penetrate the hot halo ( Dekel and Birnboim 2006 ) . Consequently, the thermodynamical state of the hot gas and its regulation by AGN feedback play a key role in controlling the star formation activity of massive galaxies. In this work, we compare three state-of-the-art cosmological hydrodynamical simulations: IllustrisTNG ( Pillepich et al. 2018a ; Nelson et al. 2018 ) , SIMBA ( Davé et al. 2019 ) , and Magneticum ( Dolag et al. 2016 ; Dolag et al. 2025 ) . The comparison is motivated by their markedly different levels of agreement with current measurements of the f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{\mathrm{h}} relation from X-ray and kSZ observations: Magneticum shows the closest agreement, SIMBA provides an intermediate match, while IllustrisTNG exhibits the largest discrepancy ( Popesso, P. et al. 2026 ) . These simulations adopt different implementations of AGN feedback, ranging from dual-mode thermal and kinetic feedback in IllustrisTNG ( Weinberger et al. 2017 ; Pillepich et al. 2018a ) , jet-driven and X-ray feedback in SIMBA ( Davé et al. 2019 ) , and a highly efficient thermal feedback model in Magneticum ( Dolag et al. 2016 ; Dolag et al. 2025 ) . Taken together, they provide a controlled framework for testing whether models that successfully reproduce the hot gas content of halos can also recover the observed distribution of galaxy properties. To enable a fair and robust comparison between simulations and observations, we adopt the f gas f_{\mathrm{gas}} – M h M_{\mathrm{h}} relations from Popesso, P. et al. (2026) and Siegel et al. (2026) (see appendix Fig. 9 ), and use MaNGA as our primary low-redshift benchmark for galaxy properties. MaNGA provides spatially resolved integral-field spectroscopy for a statistically representative sample of nearby galaxies with stellar masses M ⋆ > 10 10 ​ M ⊙ M_{\star}>10^{10}\,M_{\odot} , enabling accurate measurements of star formation rates (SFR) and stellar masses while minimising aperture biases. Its dense sampling of group environments, where the majority of galaxies reside in the local Universe, makes it particularly well suited for comparisons with cosmological simulations. Section 3 examines the distribution of galaxies on the SFR– M ⋆ M_{\star} plane and compares quenching fractions between observations and simulations. Section 4 investigates the distribution of AGN activity, while Section 5 explores the environmental dependence of galaxy evolution. Finally, Section 6 summarises our results and conclusively highlighting their implications for models of baryon cycling in the local Universe.
